extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics and classical geometry; advanced readers interested in Greek geometric constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and reconstruct classical Greek neusis problems and related constructions (plane vs solid), methods for solving quadratics and cubics, and the criteria that determine when straightedge-and-compass suffices or when conics (or mechanical equivalents) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the νεῦσις (neusis) problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any two straight lines forming an angle and any fixed point which is not on either line, it is required to draw through the fixed point a straight line such that the portion of it intercepted between the fixed lines is equal to a given length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical geometric setup: label fixed lines AE, AC and fixed point B; complete a parallelogram and introduce an auxiliary point P so that the desired intercept equals the given length. In the general solution P is found as an intersection of (1) a circle (centre at C with radius the given length) and (2) a rectangular hyperbola with given asymptotes (e.g. DH, DB). Examples: trisection of an angle and doubling the cube were effected via special instances of this νεῦσις.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane vs 'solid' problems criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem is 'plane' if it can be solved by straight line and circle (straightedge-and-compass) methods; it is 'solid' if it requires conics (or a mechanical equivalent) for its solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to classify neusis cases and other classical problems. The general νεῦσις is 'solid' (requires conics), but special configurations (e.g. fixed point on an angle bisector making the parallelogram a rhombus or square) reduce it to a 'plane' problem solvable by ruler and compass. Historical sources (Pappus, Apollonius) single out such plane cases explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the νεῦσις reduces to a 'plane' problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The νεῦσις reduces to plane methods when the fixed point lies on one of the bisectors of the angle between the two given straight lines (equivalently, when the parallelogram ACBD is a rhombus or a square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus lists the rhombus (and implicitly the square) as plane cases. The text explains constructions for both: Apollonius' construction for a rhombus (involving a circle with centre E and radius EF) and Heraclitus' construction for the square (using semicircle on BF as diameter). The reduction often relies on special equalities (e.g. EF mean proportional between BE and EC) that permit straightedge-and-compass constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General solution by intersection of a circle and a rectangular hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: In the general νεῦσις, after suitable parallelogram completions, the auxiliary point P lies at one of the intersections of (1) a circle with centre at one vertex and radius equal to the given length and (2) the rectangular hyperbola passing through that vertex with specified asymptotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction procedure: complete parallelograms to identify point P; draw the circle (centre D, radius k) and the rectangular hyperbola with asymptotes BR, BA passing through D; their intersection gives P, then draw PR parallel to DC to obtain the required intercept AQF. This shows why conics are necessary in the general case and clarifies the geometric locus interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane constructions that avoid conics (square case / Heraclitus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific constructions (e.g. Heraclitus' for a square) yield plane solutions using semicircles and similarity: construct BF so that CF^2 = BC^2 + EH^2 (with EH equal to the given intercept length); then the semicircle on BF meets AD produced in E giving HE equal to the given length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise method: (1) form a square equal to BC^2 + k^2 to get CF, (2) extend BC to F with CF equal to that side, (3) draw semicircle on BF, (4) intersect with AD produced to obtain E with HE = k. Use Pythagorean identities and cyclic quadrilateral arguments to verify correctness. The text provides algebraic and geometric verifications (equal triangles, right angles, concyclicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of quadratic problems and mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Quadratic geometric problems correspond to finding a mean proportional (single mean proportional) between two lengths; e.g., finding a square equal to a given rectilineal area reduces to finding a mean proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies the Greeks' ability to solve all quadratic equations with positive roots using application of areas and transformations into rectangles and squares. The pure quadratic (a^2 = ab) becomes mean proportional problem. The text references Euclid and the Pythagorean theorem (Eucl. I.47) as alternative geometric methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubling the cube equivalent to finding two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of doubling the cube (or extracting cube roots) is equivalent to finding two mean proportionals between two given straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If x and y are two mean proportionals between a and b, then a:x = x:y = y:b leads to relations giving the cube root. Historical note: Hippocrates' reduction and Menaechmus' conic constructions provided geometric solutions of this type. This is the reason why problems involving cube-related ratios generally require conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics to solve cubic equations and determine number of real roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Cubic equations (and related solid problems) are solved geometrically by intersections of conics (e.g. parabola and rectangular hyperbola); such geometric analysis also yields the possible number of positive real solutions (0, 1, or 2 in the contexts discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes reduced certain division-of-volume problems to a cubic and solved them by intersecting a parabola and rectangular hyperbola; he also carried out the necessary διορισμός (investigation) to determine ranges producing 0,1,2 real roots. Menaechmus' constructions for pure cubics use x = a y and cy = ab (parabola and hyperbola). Dionysodorus and others present variations with specific parameters; the method both constructs solutions and clarifies multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Διορισμός (diorismos) — investigation of existence and parameter limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some problems require a διορισμός — an explicit investigation of the limits/conditions under which a real (geometrical) solution exists, and how many solutions there are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Archimedes' treatment of the cubic arising from sphere division investigates the maximum admissible value of parameters (e.g. maximum of x^2(a−2)) to determine when real solutions occur; Pappus' rhombus case needs a διορισμός to identify a minimum k for solvability. Such analysis is part of the solution, not an optional addendum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting / detecting multiple solutions by intersection loci
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersections of conics (or conics with circles) provide a geometric way to observe existence of multiple solutions or the impossibility of solution: the number of intersection points corresponds to the number of genuine geometric solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apollonius emphasised using intersections to 'afford a more ready means of observing some things', for example that several solutions are possible, or none. He applied this to determine numbers of normals to conics (via intersections with a rectangular hyperbola) and other problems where multiplicity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for direct geometric methods over algebraic reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek geometers (e.g. Apollonius) typically solved problems by direct geometric constructions and locus reasoning rather than reducing them to algebraic cubic equations, because drawing the conics in the figure rendered an explicit algebraic detour unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological stance explains why Apollonius treats many cases geometrically even if an algebraic cubic could be written; it also explains variations in exposition among authors (Archimedes presents the cubic explicitly when no conic was in the original figure). Use this criterion when reconstructing historical solutions: prefer direct geometric locus/conic reasoning if present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of constructions via similarity, congruence, and cyclicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical constructions are verified by establishing equal angles, equal sides (similarity/congruence), and cyclic quadrilaterals, often using parallelogram-complements, equal triangles, and right-angle properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus' proofs use comparisons of triangles, parallels, and properties of circles to show that constructed points lie on intended lines (e.g. proving BKH is a straight line). When reconstructing or checking a construction, follow the chain: show equal angles or equal segments → deduce similarity/congruence → infer cyclicity or straightness as required.
